Estimating physics from images: what real measurements reveal

Community Article Published
October 16, 2026 Upvote 8 Luca Cilio lucakae projectsim
Reconstructing an object's 3D shape and appearance from images leaves its mass and contact properties unresolved. In physics engines such as PhysX and MuJoCo, those properties affect how the object responds when a robot pushes, grasps or drops it [8].
We evaluated ProjectSim’s image-based physical property estimates against measurements from three research datasets: YCB, NeRF2Physics and IDPP. The comparisons cover mass, sliding friction, indentation hardness and restitution, which describes rebound at impact. Our mass and friction estimates agreed more closely with the measurements than the simple density and constant-value assignments we tested. We also evaluated restitution from a single still frame against references obtained from recorded motion.
A separate experiment examined how friction values should be assigned to an asset. An object can have different measured friction on different surfaces, so one coefficient used directly for every contact cannot express all of those measurements. We fitted two ways of assigning coefficients to known contact measurements, examining this limitation separately from the accuracy of image-based estimates.

Comparing estimates with measurements

ProjectSim builds 3D assets from images and uses a vision-language model to estimate physical properties from rendered views of the resulting asset. The four evaluations use different sources of ground truth: scale measurements for objects in the YCB collection [1], sliding friction and indentation hardness measurements from NeRF2Physics [2], and bounce recordings from IDPP [3].
To score agreement, we use the min ratio error (MnRE) metric used in NeRF2Physics and PhysGS [2, 4]. Higher scores mean closer agreement. For a positive reference value p and a nonnegative estimate p̂, the score is the smaller value divided by the larger:
MnRE⁡(p^,p)=min⁡(p^,p)max⁡(p^,p).
\operatorname{MnRE}(\hat p,p)=\frac{\min(\hat p,p)}{\max(\hat p,p)}.
MnRE(p^​,p)=max(p^​,p)min(p^​,p)​.
An exact estimate scores 1; an estimate twice or half the reference scores 0.5. We report the mean across the evaluated items.
The mass comparisons come from our reruns of selected research methods. The friction and hardness comparisons use the external results published in PhysGS [4].

Baselines: density and constant values

We compared the estimates with three simple parameter assignments. For mass, we tested an assumed density multiplied by the volume of the 3D mesh. For friction, we assigned 0.5 to every tested contact. For restitution, we assigned zero, corresponding to no rebound along the direction perpendicular to the contact surface. Those friction and restitution values appear in Isaac Lab's documented material defaults [10].

Mass: agreement with scale measurements

For a broader comparison, we reran four research methods on YCB objects and scored their mass estimates against measurements from a digital scale. ProjectSim achieved the highest mean MnRE in this comparison (Table 3). We then examined individual predictions and found that 51 of 61 predicted masses were within a factor of two of the measured mass (Figure 2).

Friction and hardness: interpreting the measurements

The coefficient of kinetic friction is the sliding friction force divided by the normal force, the force perpendicular to the contact surface. The NeRF2Physics reference measurements used an iOLab cart fitted with fabric pads on six surfaces [2]. Each coefficient describes a fabric-pad–surface contact.
On those six contacts, our mean MnRE was 0.833. PhysGS reports 0.805, alongside the NeRF2Physics, CLIP and GPT-4V comparisons reproduced in Table 4 [4].

Fitting friction to object–surface pairs

To separate the choice of coefficients from image inference, we examined another set of measured contacts. In IDPP, objects were pulled across horizontal surfaces at steady speed with a spring dynamometer, giving the kinetic-friction coefficient as pulling force divided by weight [3]. Our diagnostic used 28 measured contacts involving five objects and six surfaces. The same LEGO brick had different measured friction on paperboard and on a grey towel. One coefficient attached to the brick cannot reproduce both contacts directly.
The OpenUSD physics schema stores friction coefficients on materials and describes combining the coefficients of contacting materials, including by averaging [9]. We fitted two representations to the known measurements and scored them on those same contacts. Assigning one coefficient per object gave a mean MnRE of 0.794. Assigning five object coefficients and six surface coefficients, with each contact predicted by their arithmetic mean, gave 0.931:
μ^ij=ai+bj2,
\hat\mu_{ij}=\frac{a_i+b_j}{2},
μ^​ij​=2ai​+bj​​,
where aᵢ is the fitted coefficient for object i and bⱼ is the fitted coefficient for surface j.
The second representation has more freedom to capture differences between contacts and fits these measurements more closely. To validate estimates for this representation, we need to compare the combined contact coefficient with the real measurement.

Hardness: resistance to indentation

The hardness evaluation uses Shore durometer readings at 31 measurement points on 11 NeRF2Physics objects [2]. Shore A and Shore D use different scales and indenters.
For the published comparisons, NeRF2Physics and PhysGS use an index that leaves Shore A readings unchanged and maps a Shore D reading to 100 + D [2, 4]. Our hardness evaluation reports 0.807, compared with PhysGS's published 0.839.

Restitution: estimates from a single still frame

The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the relative normal separation speed after impact to the relative normal approach speed before impact.
For this evaluation, the reference coefficients came from tracked bounce recordings in IDPP [3]. In an ideal vertical drop from rest onto a stationary surface, neglecting air resistance, the coefficient is the square root of the ratio of rebound height to drop height. Our estimator received one still frame per retained clip. It achieved a mean MnRE of 0.880 over 77 clips, primarily showing balls.

Conclusion

Our mass and friction estimates were closer to real measurements than the simple baselines and the research methods compared here. We also obtained close agreement for restitution using one still frame per clip. For robotics teams, these results point towards simulations that better reflect the objects a robot will handle. Better estimates could help recreate how those objects respond to a push, grasp or drop.
As we improve our ability to create 3D objects with realistic physical properties, we want robotics teams to be able to use simulation for more of their training. Reproducing a wider range of real interactions could give robots more varied practice, helping them learn, adapt and improve before they face the real world.
